Source. In the `case '.'` precision parser, `mrb_str_format()` calls `get_num()` on the attacker-controlled digit run after `.` in `%.4294629629s`, materializing that decimal text as numeric precision state.
The digit loop consumes `4294629629` into `mrb_int next_n`. On this build `mrb_int` is wide enough that neither overflow check fires, so `next_n` ends the loop as the positive value `4294629629`.

Root cause. Vulnerable `get_num()` narrows `next_n == 4294629629` directly into 32-bit `int`, so the parsed precision becomes `-337667` for this witness. The staged patch inserts `if (next_n > INT_MAX || next_n < 0) return NULL;` immediately before this cast to block exactly this transition.
The `%s` formatter reaches its precision-truncation branch because `FPREC` is set for `%.4294629629s` and the narrowed `prec` is negative while `slen = RSTRING_LEN(str)` is non-negative.

Inside that branch, the negative precision is propagated into the derived copy state: the temporary pointer moves backward from the string base, `slen` is overwritten with the same negative value, and `len` becomes the same negative offset that will later be used as the copy length.

The width-handling branch is not taken on this witness because the malformed specifier provided precision but no width, so `FWIDTH` is clear and execution falls through toward the unconditional final `PUSH` at line 841.

#define CHECK(l) do {                           \
  while ((l) >= bsiz - blen) {\
    if (bsiz > MRB_INT_MAX/2) mrb_raise(mrb, E_ARGUMENT_ERROR, "too big specifier"); \
    bsiz*=2;\
  }\
  mrb_str_resize(mrb, result, bsiz);\
  buf = RSTRING_PTR(result);\
} while (0)
